newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Turkey, Turkish Cypriots look to "integration".
newsitem.headline: Turkey, Turkish Cypriots look to "integration".

text.p: Turkey on Sunday marked the anniversary of its 1974 invasion of Cyprus with a call for the "partial integration" with the island's occupied north.

Turkish deputy Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit, who as prime minister originally ordered the invasion, said integration of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) was inevitable after the European Union gave a green light last week to Cyprus for membership and excluded Turkey.
"The TRNC will live forever as an independent state. But its foreign policy and defence will be handled by Turkey," Ecevit told an anniversary ceremony.
A joint declaration issued by Turkey and the Turkish Cypriots outlined a proposed series of steps toward integration, including efforts on defence, foreign and economic policies.
Most of what was in the declaration is already in effect today. Turkey maintains 30,000 troops in the north.
"Any attack on the TRNC will be considered as an attack on the Republic of Turkey. In this context, a joint defence concept will be established between Turkey and the TRNC," the statement said.

Ankara says allowing Cyprus, run by a Greek Cypriot government that is internationally recognised, to join the EU before solving the division of the island would only reinforce the tensions between the Greek and Turkish Cypriots.
"The world must understand that Turkey is not bluffing. It proved in 1974 that it does not bluff," Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash said at the ceremony.
Turkey invaded the northern third of the island on July 20, 1974, in response to a short-lived Greek Cypriot coup backed by the military then ruling Greece.
Cyprus has since been divided into Greek and Turkish Cypriot sectors. The breakaway TRNC was declared in 1983 but is recognised only by Ankara.
Denktash criticised Greek Cypriot arms purchases and accused the Greek Cypriot administration of dragging its feet in peace talks.
Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides said on Saturday he was willing to negotiate in a spirit of goodwill to reunite the eastern Mediterranean island.
But he added that he would not accept a solution that would compromise the existence of Greek Cypriots.
Clerides recently met Denktash in New York state in an attempt to revive stalled negotiations on reunification as a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.
Clerides and Denktash have agreed to meet in the Cyprus capital Nicosia before the second round to discuss humanitarian issues.
Turkish Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz, meanwhile, pledged continued support for Turkish Cypriots.
"Our government will continue to contribute efforts by Turkish Cypriots for development and higher welfare level," Yilmaz was quoted by Anatoilian news agency.
In the Greek Cypriot-populated south flags flew at half mast and church bells tolled in mourning at midday.
Earlier, at 5.20 a.m. (0220 GMT) air raid sirens sounded over the divided capital Nicosia, marking the hour when Turkish forces first landed on the island 23 years ago.

At Nicosia's Ledra Palace, a United Nations-controlled checkpoint between the north and south of the island, dozens of black-clad Greek Cypriot women silently sat in the burning heat clutching yellowed pictures in large frames, demanding to know the fate of relatives missing since the invasion.
"Yiannakis went missing on the first day of the invasion... he was only 14," wept his mother, Maroulla Kozakos.
The Greek Cypriots say the fate of some 1,619 persons who went missing during the invasion is unaccounted for.
